Macrolide resistance as high as 35% has been re- ported in some areas of the USA and Europe; 96% resist- ance has been reported in Taiwan. Fluoroquinolone resistance was low overall (1%) although 14.3% of iso- lates were resistant in Hong Kong.9,10 However, in clinical practice pneumococcal pneumonia frequently responds to high doses of penicillins or cephalosporins and the routine use of penicillin for community-acquired pneumonia may still be reasonable in many countries. The treatment of community-acquired pneumonia is com- plicated by the increasing spectrum of causative organisms and prevalence of antibacterial resistance. Furthermore, since the causative pathogen is often unknown, initial an- tibacterial therapy is usually empirical. Guidelines for the treatment of pneumonia have been issued by bodies in many countries.8,11-18 Although common principles can be identified, recommendations must be localised because of differences in patterns of infection and drug resistance, variations in the availability of antibacterials and local Antibacterials 187 The symbol † denotes a preparation no longer actively marketed The symbol  denotes a substance whose use may be restricted in certain sports (see p.vii) policies for their use, and differences in medical practice. Countries also vary in the degree to which such guidelines are accepted in practice. These guidelines generally give advice for differences associated with age, the severity of the infection and the presence or absence of underlying or co-existent disorders. In the UK, guidelines for the management of community- acquired pneumonia have been produced by the British Thoracic Society (BTS).8 For initial empirical treatment in the community amoxicillin is usually preferred. Eryth- romycin is an alternative in penicillin-allergic patients and should also be given during epidemics of mycoplasmal pneumonia and when Legionella is suspected; clarithro- mycin may be given if there is gastrointestinal intolerance to erythromycin.
